text: The hob is a British and Scottish folkloric figure. Writers also call it hobtrust, hobtrush, and hobgoblin. The syllable hob appears in many words linked to fairies. It may be a short form of Robert, a name given to English brownies or helpful household spirits. Robin Goodfellow comes from the same stem. In northern Britain the hob was a kind spirit. It helped local people with healing and farm work. A person could never reward the hob. A reward would scare it off. Less kindly hobs also appear in folklore. Hob Headless haunted a road near the River Kent. Confined under a rock for 99 years, it trapped people who rested on the rock and glued them down. Hobgoblin is a generic name for malicious spirits. In Scotland hobgoblins caused distress for their own sake. They took ominous forms to terrify night walkers, even making a haystack seem alive. Some legends say such an apparition foretold death.
